Johann Eck
yō´hän ĕk
n. (Johann Maier von Eck, 1486–1543, professor at Ingolstadt and Luther's most formidable Roman antagonist, who forced the issue of papal authority at the Leipzig Disputation of 1519)
German Eck, a corner, from his birthplace Egg an der Günz; his family name was Maier.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johann Eck was a brilliant and combative theologian who understood Luther's position earlier and better than most of its defenders. At Leipzig in 1519 he set out to prove that the Wittenberg case entailed consequences Luther had not yet admitted, and he succeeded: pressed on the authority of the pope, Luther conceded that the papacy is of human institution, that councils may err, and that Jan Hus had been condemned for holding articles that are plainly scriptural. Eck had drawn the real line into the open, and both sides afterwards knew what the quarrel was about. He went to Rome, helped procure the bull Exsurge Domine, published it in Germany, and spent the next twenty years in controversy, drafting the Confutatio against the Augsburg Confession in 1530. Pro 18:17 is the honest comment on a disputation — “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” — and Eck was a searching neighbour. But Gal 1:8 is the standard he failed: a gospel other than the apostolic one is accursed “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach” it, and no see's authority alters that.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a disputation as a contest in words; controversy; an exercise in colleges, in which parties reason in opposition to each other.

expand to see more

DISPUTA'TION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something.

2. A contest in words; controversy.

3. An exercise in colleges, in which parties reason in opposition to each other, on some question proposed.

Key Scripture

Act 4:12 — "Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved."

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Pro 18:17 — "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him."

1Pe 2:6 — "Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded."

Modern Corruption

Eck did the Reformation an unintended service by forcing it to say out loud that the papacy is of human institution.

expand to see more

Luther went to Leipzig still hoping the quarrel could be settled within the existing authority, and Eck would not let him. By pressing the logic — if indulgences are indefensible, who defended them? and if a council erred at Constance, what is a council? — he compelled a clarity that the Wittenberg party had been avoiding. Rome gained a polemicist and lost the possibility of a quiet settlement. 1Pe 2:6 names the only foundation on offer: “Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious,” and the stone is Christ, not a succession.

Eck's own error is the one his whole career defends: that the authority of the church guarantees the doctrine, so that what Rome teaches must be what Scripture means. Act 4:12 will not bear it — “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” — and a system that adds merit, treasury and indulgence to that name has added another way. The recovery is to welcome a sharp opponent, since a searching neighbour exposes what a man really holds, and then to answer him from the text rather than from an office.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek onoma (G3686), a name; anathema (G331), accursed; Hebrew rib (H7379), a cause, a dispute.

Greek onoma (G3686) — a name, hence authority; Acts 4:12.

Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.

Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to preach good tidings; Galatians 1:8.

Hebrew rib (H7379) — a cause, a controversy; Proverbs 18:17.

Usage

"“there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12) — the name no office supplements."

"“though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel” (Gal 1:8) — the standard above every see."

"“He that is first in his own cause seemeth just” (Pro 18:17) — the use of a searching opponent."
